## Testing

Add replay-specific size-limit tests and enlarge the Bash integration-test snapshot to exercise file replay beyond the environment replay budget.

items.body:
## Environment

- Codex desktop on macOS, with a cloud parent dot conversation delegating work to tasks on the connected Mac.
- Exact Codex app version, macOS version and model configuration were not captured in the evidence used for this report.
- Observed during an ongoing workflow on October 5–6, 2026.

## What happened

I explicitly approved a bounded data transfer in the parent conversation, including the data category, destination and purpose. The parent retrieved that approval and its preceding question through the supported authenticated conversation reader, then forwarded the returned evidence to the existing local task. Automatic review still rejected the delegated action because the relayed evidence did not establish trusted user authorization.

For the NotebookLM operation, repeating the same scoped permission directly in the local task subsequently allowed progress: the task reported updating two existing sources and reading the results back. This created an extra manual approval step even though the parent had already verified the user's answer.

The failure being reported is the lack of a usable, verifiable consent handoff across this delegation boundary. The underlying implementation cause is unknown.

## Minimal observed sequence

This is a reduced description of the recorded workflow; a fresh isolated reproduction has not been run.

1. A parent dot delegates a task to the connected Mac. The task needs to update specified existing NotebookLM sources.
2. In the parent conversation, the user explicitly approves the bounded content, destination and purpose.
3. The parent reads the actual user reply together with the exact approval question using its authenticated conversation reader, then forwards that evidence unchanged to the existing local task.
4. The delegated guarded attempt is rejected before process creation. No new source update or consultation occurs during that rejected attempt.
5. The user repeats the same scoped authorization directly in the local task's conversation. The parent verifies that a native user message exists there.
6. The task then reports successful updates and readback of two existing sources. No new consultation is claimed.

## Second observed case: Drive upload

A later approval explicitly covered two named payloads and one Drive destination. After the parent retrieved that fresh approval:

- The parent's upload of a sanitized conversation archive succeeded, with full provider readback.
- A local task's source-archive upload was denied after receiving the authenticated parent approval verbatim. The task reported that review treated the source transfer, destination and forwarded authorization as insufficiently trusted. That attempt produced no upload or readback, and the task stopped.
- The user then approved that exact archive and destination directly in the local task. The parent verified the native user message. The task reported a successful upload and full matching provider readback; the parent also independently downloaded the provider archive and verified its hash.

These were different payloads and execution contexts. The differing outcomes do not establish why review handled them differently.

## Expected behavior

Provide a supported consent handoff that lets review verify the original authenticated human approval, its scope and the intended delegated action. Bind it to the approved data, destination and task, and preserve revocation and other applicable checks.

If this kind of consent cannot cross the parent/task boundary, expose that limitation and a working approval path in the coordinating conversation. Users should not have to discover which child conversation must receive the same approval again.

Arbitrary quoted text must remain untrusted. This request does not ask to bypass safety review or broaden a user's approval.

## Evidence and limits

The account above is based on the parent's authenticated reads of user messages and its reads of completed local-task reports. The NotebookLM writes and readback are reported outcomes. The successful source-archive transfer also has a parent-verified full provider download and hash comparison. This public report does not include the full native receipts. The exact rejection wording is paraphrased, and no reviewer internals or root cause are claimed. The observations do not establish that every delegated task is affected.

The immediate impact was repeated user intervention and delayed authorized work. No billing or total lost-time estimate is claimed. Private conversation text, project identities, source contents, resource identifiers, credentials and raw logs are omitted.

## Related reports

- [#50794](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/50794): forwarded approval rejected on Windows, with an additional failure to enter approval in the original task. Native input worked for the NotebookLM case here.
- [#41706](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/41706): scoped consent provenance across task creation and a separate parent-return channel concern. This report adds an existing macOS delegated task receiving evidence from an authenticated parent conversation read.
- [#45470](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/45470): delegated desktop communication rejected as untrusted authorization, including a reported direct-approval case.
- [#49417](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/49417): authorization originating in a voice call rejected for a Slack action.
- [#49883](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/49883): broader macOS delegation continuation and approval-handoff stalls.

These reports have related symptoms; a shared root cause has not been established. Please consolidate this report with an existing issue if it belongs to the same defect, and identify the supported way to pass verifiable scoped consent.

### What version of the Codex App are you using (From "About Codex" dialog)?

Codex Desktop package `OpenAI.Codex 26.930.7945.0` (verified from the installed Windows package).
Affected session runtime: `codex-cli 0.160.1`.
Model: `gpt-6.1-sol`, reasoning effort: `high`.

### What subscription do you have?

Not included in this report.

### What platform is your computer?

Microsoft Windows 11 Pro, version `10.0.26300`, build `26300`, x64.
Native local Windows workspace; PowerShell 7 was used for the observed shell calls.

### What issue are you seeing?

On October 6, 2026, an ordinary, newly started local Codex Desktop task produced a user-visible response that the user described as garbage instead of a usable answer. The user explicitly clarified that the complaint concerns the answer content, rather than a failed PowerShell command.

The exact garbled text could not be recovered from either the native thread inspection API or the matching local rollout JSONL. I am not supplying a reconstructed or invented excerpt.

The available persisted evidence is:
- The session starts with a normal Polish request to find an existing software support ticket and identify where a template correction belongs in an upcoming development version.
- One coherent assistant commentary message is persisted.
- Two shell executions follow. The first completed with exit code 0 in 119 ms; the second completed with exit code 1 in 285 ms. Their outputs included large text reads, with truncation visible in native inspection.
- At inspection, the native thread API reports the turn as `inProgress`, with `error: null`, and does not expose the garbage response or a final answer.
- All records in the inspected local JSONL parse successfully; it contains no persisted assistant `final_answer` with the reported garbage.

This is a user-visible corruption report with a persistence/inspection evidence gap. The available evidence does not establish whether generation, streaming, message classification, or desktop rendering is responsible. It also does not establish that the shell calls themselves hung or caused the corruption.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

No deterministic minimal reproducer is available. Observed sequence:
1. Start a new local task in Codex Desktop on Windows.
2. Ask in Polish to locate an existing software support ticket and identify the relevant template/development change.
3. Let Codex read local instructions and search repository files using its shell tools.
4. A garbage response is displayed instead of a usable answer.
5. Inspect the affected thread: the displayed corruption is not present in the native inspection result or the matching persisted JSONL.

Affected session ID: `01a11103-b0ed-7551-91e8-6a4bd39f3c6b`.
Affected turn ID: `01a11103-daaa-7512-9027-afcbe208f99d`.
Session start: October 6, 2026, approximately 11:40 UTC / 13:40 Europe/Warsaw.

This captured task is short and has no persisted context-compaction event. Please do not assume the long-session/compaction trigger described in some earlier reports applies here.

### What is the expected behavior?

Codex should display a coherent response to the user's request. If generation or streaming fails, it should end with an explicit recoverable error rather than present garbage as an answer. Thread inspection and persisted history should provide sufficient evidence to correlate the displayed failure with the affected turn.

### Additional information

Potentially related reports:
- #34174: corrupted desktop replies with multilingual/internal-looking fragments.
- #40957: repetitive garbage output in the Windows app.
- #37524: internal-looking planning text appearing in visible assistant messages.

A shared root cause is unconfirmed. This occurrence involves a newer Desktop/runtime build, GPT-6.1 Sol, and a newly started short local task. Please merge/deduplicate if appropriate.

No complete transcript, private project paths, support-ticket contents, customer data, credentials, or account history are attached publicly.

items.body:
### What variant of Codex are you using?

ChatGPT/Codex desktop app on Windows x64. Installed package version: 26.930.7945.0.

### What feature would you like to see?

Please allow reviewers with the necessary GitHub permissions to merge pull requests they did not author from the Code Review page.

Developers send me pull requests for review and merging. I can inspect the changes and submit an approval in the desktop app, but the Merge button is missing for their PRs. It appears for my own PRs. On the GitHub website, the affected PR offers both squash-and-merge and a merge commit, so I have to leave the app to finish the workflow.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Sign in with a GitHub account that can merge pull requests in a repository.
2. Have another developer create a PR and request your review.
3. Open that PR in the desktop app's Code Review page.
4. Review and approve it. In the observed case, the page reports “Can merge without conflicts.”
5. Observe that the toolbar offers “Submit review” but no Merge action.
6. Open the same PR on GitHub: merge actions are available.
7. Compare with a PR you authored: the desktop app exposes merge controls there.

### Expected behavior

Merge controls should be available based on the connected account's merge permissions and the PR's current state, without requiring that account to be the author. Keep the existing confirmation, allowed merge methods, checks, branch protections, and revision validation.

Submitting a review and merging are separate actions; authorized reviewers need access to both.

### Additional information

Read-only inspection of the installed app bundle found an explicit author check in the PR action component: it returns no controls when `detail.isAuthor` is false. The header also gates merge controls on authorship and displays review submission controls for non-authors. This explains the observed difference; it does not establish the product rationale.

If this restriction is intentional, please explain why it is needed and consider supporting the reviewer/maintainer workflow. The current behavior makes the integrated PR page incomplete for people responsible for both reviewing and merging their team's work.

No PR was merged during this investigation. Private repository names, PR contents, and the screenshot have been omitted.

Error: app-server control socket is already in use at ~/.codex/app-server-control/app-server-control.sock

That path is a symlink to the active /tmp/codex-daemon-<uid>/<socket-id> endpoint.

A read-only process snapshot showed a classic app-server, managed app-server/daemon, VS Code extension app-server, and app-server proxy coexisting. Some app-server-related processes had PPID 1.

After cleanup and reauthentication, Codex became usable again. Later, after another worker/task was started through the extension, approval interaction in another worker stopped functioning. While the approval was pending, the normal text-input field was also unavailable, leaving that worker effectively stuck: the action could not be approved and the worker could not be instructed to cancel or continue differently.

During this recurrence the task count was only 798/2048, and the known daemon socket remained associated with the same app-server processes. Two codex-code-mode-host processes were observed under different app-server roles.

These observations establish temporal correlation only; I have not established that starting the additional worker caused the approval failure.

A separate session-history symptom was also observed: an existing and resumable session disappeared from VS Code history while its JSONL remained present. Its index updated_at value was stale.

This is currently a recurring failure rather than a deterministic minimal reproduction.

Observed sequence:

1. Use Codex through VS Code Remote-SSH on a Linux host with a persistent/shared home directory and default CODEX_HOME (~/.codex).
2. Use Codex across multiple remote sessions/workers over time.
3. Old app-server processes may remain on the remote host, including app-server-related processes with PPID 1.
4. A subsequent Codex connection can encounter:
   "app-server control socket is already in use"
5. After recovering the environment and reauthenticating, Codex was usable again.
6. Start another worker/task through the VS Code extension.
7. In the observed recurrence, another worker subsequently entered an approval state in which the approval interaction did not function and the normal text-input field was unavailable.

During the recurrence, the user task count was 798/2048, so task-limit exhaustion was not present.

I do not currently have a deterministic minimal reproduction and do not claim that step 6 causes step 7.

### What is the expected behavior?

Remote-SSH reconnects and concurrent workers should not leave stale app-server ownership that prevents a new client from using the expected control endpoint.

If multiple app-server roles and code-mode hosts are expected to coexist, endpoint ownership, health checking, and handoff should be unambiguous.

An approval request should either remain actionable or provide a way to cancel/return to normal text input. A failed approval interaction should not leave the worker without both a functional approval control and normal text input.

Existing resumable sessions should remain discoverable in VS Code history even if an index timestamp becomes stale, or the index should be safely reconciled/rebuilt.

### Additional information

Environment details:

- Default CODEX_HOME (~/.codex)
- Persistent/shared remote home
- Remote user/process limit: 2048
- `codex --version`: codex-cli 0.160.0
- VS Code extension bundled Codex binary: codex-cli 0.160.1
- VS Code extension: openai.chatgpt-26.930.61225
- The version difference is reported for reproducibility; I do not assume that version skew itself is a bug.
- Historical log entries referenced client_version=0.153.4, but later live process inspection found no running process using a 0.153.4 path. An old 0.153.4 installation remained on disk.
- The log also contains:
  `failed to clean up stale arg0 temp dirs: Directory not empty (os error 39)`
  Its relevance is unknown.
- `codex doctor --json` independently reports `state.rollout_db_parity` as a warning: 33 active rollout files are present, but only 15 active rows exist in the state DB, leaving 18 active rollout files without matching thread rows. The doctor report describes the cause as `rollout files are missing from the state DB` and expects every rollout file to have a matching threads row.

Questions:

- Are the classic app-server, managed daemon, proxy, VS Code app-server, and multiple code-mode hosts expected to coexist on one Remote-SSH host?
- Which component owns the control endpoint, and how should stale PPID-1 app-server processes be reclaimed?
- Can multiple concurrent code-mode hosts interfere with approval routing to the correct VS Code client/worker?
- Is there a supported mechanism to reconcile/rebuild the session/thread state when rollout JSONL files exist but corresponding state-DB thread rows are missing?

I can provide sanitized process/socket details privately if needed. Raw session JSONLs, authentication material, account identifiers, and unrelated session contents have intentionally not been included.

## Summary
The Windows ChatGPT/Codex desktop app repeatedly becomes unresponsive and its UI resets. This affects multiple existing chats and can also prevent using the New chat UI, making normal work impossible. Relaunching does not provide a lasting recovery.

## Environment
- Component: Windows desktop app (Codex view)
- Installed app version reported by the app updater: 26.930.61225, build 13232, production channel; updater reported up_to_date.
- Selected model in the affected chats: gpt-6.1-sol.
- Observed again on October 6, 2026, evening in Asia/Seoul.
- Physical RAM: 31.77 GB. A recent snapshot showed 70.6% used and 9.34 GB free. This was NOT a measurement at the exact failure instant.

## User-observed behavior
1. Open the Windows desktop app and continue working in existing chats.
2. The app becomes sluggish, stops responding, and the visible UI resets. This has occurred repeatedly in more than one chat.
3. The New chat UI can become unusable too, so starting a smaller conversation is not an available workaround during the failure.
4. Closing and reopening the app does not prevent recurrence.

The user reports worse behavior from evening through early morning, and worsening after the GPT-6.1 Sol update. These are observations, not an established model-related cause. A controlled cross-model or browser comparison has not been completed; no exact deterministic trigger is established.

## Expected behavior
Existing chats, navigation, and New chat remain responsive. Large histories should not make the entire application unusable. Recovery should preserve local work and conversation records.

## Sanitized local diagnostic findings
- In one observed recovery sequence, the main process remained alive while renderer processes disappeared or were recreated. This alone does not establish a renderer crash reason.
- An earlier confirmed renderer had approximately 4 GB working-set memory. Later snapshots are from different processes, so this is NOT a demonstrated memory-leak growth curve.
- The current app log showed repeated local history access: 7,578 thread/items/list calls for one chat and 1,325 history-page events over approximately 36 minutes. Normal pagination/scrolling has not been excluded; these are NOT external model API-call counts.
- Logged UI messages included:
  - ResizeObserver loop completed with undelivered notifications.
  - React root render requested.
  - Received item/started or item/completed for unknown conversation.
  - Conversation state not found.
- Three affected chats have large on-disk rollout records (approximately 2.9 GB, 2.8 GB, and 1.5 GB). These sizes include tool/media payloads; they are NOT prompt-token counts or app RAM consumption.
- No explicit OOM or renderer-crash reason was found in the inspected app logs, and no matching Windows Application crash/hang event was found in the sampled interval. This does not rule out a UI hang or transient resource pressure.
- codex doctor --summary reported installation consistent, healthy state databases, agreeing thread inventory, successful desktop app-server initialization, HTTP reachability, and a connected WebSocket. It reported 0 failed checks, plus optional MCP configuration and non-interactive terminal warnings. These point-in-time checks do not validate renderer stability, and the warnings are not established causes.

## Related reports / request
The symptom family may overlap with #41166, but the cause and duplicate status are not established. This report adds a current 26.930.61225 recurrence affecting app-wide navigation and New chat.

Please investigate desktop history-loading/rendering/state recovery, provide a supported non-destructive mitigation, and advise how to collect targeted crash/hang diagnostics when the app UI itself is unusable. The public report intentionally excludes email addresses, chat identifiers/titles, private transcripts, credentials, local user paths, and raw logs. No destructive reset, cache deletion, or security-setting change has been performed.

items.body:
### What version of Codex CLI is running?

0.160.1

### What subscription do you have?

enterprise

### Which model were you using?

gpt-6.1-sol

### What platform is your computer?

Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS, Linux 7.0.0 aarch64

### What terminal emulator and version are you using (if applicable)?

bash

### Codex doctor report

```json

```

### What issue are you seeing?

## Summary

When a configured streamable-HTTP MCP server that uses OAuth can't be reached (in my case, its hostname doesn't resolve while I'm off my corporate VPN), the Codex TUI never starts the session. Every message I send shows up under **"• Queued follow-up inputs"** and is never run. Nothing errors out and nothing times out, and `startup_timeout_sec` has no effect.

The first launch after setting things up sometimes works. Later launches hang every time.

## Environment

- Codex CLI: `codex-cli 0.160.1` (managed daemon package `0.160.1-aarch64-unknown-linux-musl`)
- OS: Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS, Linux 7.0.0 aarch64
- Auth: ChatGPT login
- Secret storage: gnome-keyring (`org.freedesktop.secrets` over D-Bus)
- Terminal: xterm-256color (also reproduced inside tmux 3.4)

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

## Config that reproduces it

Hostnames below are redacted.

```toml
[mcp_servers.server_a]
url = "https://<internal-host>/mcp/a"

[mcp_servers.server_b]
url = "https://<internal-host>/mcp/b"

[mcp_servers.server_c]
url = "https://<internal-host>/mcp/c"

[mcp_servers.server_c.oauth]
client_id = "<redacted>"
callback_url = "http://127.0.0.1/callback/<redacted>"
```

All three servers had been authenticated via OAuth earlier (while on VPN), so their tokens are stored in the system keyring.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Configure one or more OAuth-protected HTTP MCP servers and log in to them while their host is reachable.
2. Disconnect from the network that makes the host reachable (DNS lookups for the host now time out after ~20s instead of resolving).
3. Run `codex` (or `codex --no-daemon`).
4. Type any prompt and press Enter.

### What is the expected behavior?

## Expected

The MCP server fails to start (after `startup_timeout_sec`, or after DNS/connect failure), a warning is shown, and the prompt runs without that server.

## Actual

- The prompt appears under "Queued follow-up inputs" and is never run (I waited over 100 seconds).
- No thread/session is created.
- The process is idle: no CPU use, all threads parked in `futex` or `epoll` wait. This looks like an async deadlock or an await with no timeout, not slow I/O.
- Happens both with the managed app-server daemon and with `--no-daemon`.
- With the daemon, the daemon stops logging right after startup, and `codex app-server daemon stop` itself hangs (only SIGTERM stops it).

### Additional information

## Isolation

Each run below used a fresh `CODEX_HOME` with only `auth.json` and a config variant. The system keyring is still shared between runs.

| Config | Result |
|---|---|
| No MCP servers | works |
| Only a stdio MCP server (`docker run …`) | works |
| Only `server_a` (OAuth HTTP, host unreachable) | **hangs** |
| Only `server_b` (OAuth HTTP, host unreachable) | **hangs** |
| Only `server_c` (OAuth HTTP with `[oauth]` block, host unreachable) | **hangs** |
| Only a never-authenticated HTTP server at `https://does-not-exist.invalid/mcp` (DNS also takes ~20s to fail) | works |
| `startup_timeout_sec = 5` on the three servers | **still hangs** |
| Full config with `-c mcp_servers.<name>.enabled=false` for the three servers | works |

Because a never-authenticated server with equally slow DNS works, slow DNS alone isn't the trigger. The hang seems tied to servers that have stored OAuth credentials, perhaps while loading tokens from the keyring or refreshing them against the unreachable host. This is my guess and is unconfirmed. If so, it would also explain why a first launch sometimes works and later ones don't.

Related log lines from earlier runs (daemon stderr / `logs_2.sqlite`):

```
WARN codex_rmcp_client::oauth::resolved_store ... (during thread/start)
ERROR rmcp::transport::worker: worker quit with fatal: Transport channel closed, when AuthRequired(AuthRequiredError { www_authenticate_header: "Bearer error=\"invalid_token\" ..." })
```

The hanging `--no-daemon` process wrote no log lines at all after TUI startup.

## Workaround

Disable the unreachable servers for the session:

```sh
codex -c mcp_servers.server_a.enabled=false -c mcp_servers.server_b.enabled=false -c mcp_servers.server_c.enabled=false
```

## Suggested fix

Make MCP startup (including OAuth token loading/refresh and discovery) fully bounded by `startup_timeout_sec`. Also, don't block turn submission on a server that is failing or stuck: mark it failed, show a warning, and continue.

On two Codex-managed worktrees in private repositories, Desktop startup cleanup selected a checkout associated with an unfinished chat. For one checkout, logs show two distinct `worker-start force=true reason=startup-cleanup` events. Each captured a committed-HEAD snapshot, then logged `git-remove-result code=0 success=true` and `worker-success`; the checkout became unavailable and required restoration. In a separate cleanup attempt involving another checkout, `git worktree remove --force` exited 128, but the Desktop worker still reported success. A bounded check of the source chat found no assistant-issued archive or removal command. The committed-HEAD snapshots do not prove recovery of former untracked or needed ignored bytes; that recovery remains unknown. This report omits private paths, repository names, worktree/thread IDs, and raw logs.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

This was observed during normal Desktop startup cleanup, not intentionally reproduced against real work. With automatic worktree deletion enabled, the app selected a managed checkout associated with an unfinished chat during startup. The log sequence was `worker-start force=true reason=startup-cleanup` -> snapshot of committed HEAD -> Git removal result -> worker success. A separate attempt logged Git removal exit 128 followed by worker success. Please reproduce only with disposable fixtures containing a locked worktree, an attached idle chat, untracked and needed ignored sentinels, and a simulated Git removal failure. Test both clean removal and failure paths, including selection-to-removal races. I have not rerun destructive cleanup against retained worktrees.

An unfinished chat's source checkout should not become unavailable without a clear, recoverable custody transition. A failed Git removal must fail closed; it must not be followed by recursive deletion or a success result. Snapshot/restore must preserve tracked, untracked, and needed ignored bytes plus Git registration, lock, ref, and chat attachment state. If idle-chat eviction is intended, the UI should make its scope and data-preservation guarantees explicit and offer an exact opt-out before removing an unfinished checkout.

Automatic worktree deletion is currently disabled in Settings as a mitigation. No controlled fresh-start or crash-recovery acceptance is claimed. ### What issue are you seeing?

A fresh read-only check on October 6, 2026 shows that a cloud-started/delegated task can run on the connected Windows computer and use its local Codex in-app browser, but cannot start native Windows desktop observation or control. This report isolates the remaining native desktop capability gap.

Observed in that delegated task:
- `cua_repl` is callable, but its tool description explicitly states that native computer APIs are disabled.
- No callable `node_repl` is exposed. The installed Computer Use skill is readable and instructs using `node_repl` with `@oai/sky`, so its documented native initialization route cannot be run.
- `cua.getState()` reports `apps: []`. Its initial browser inventory was also empty.
- A supported `cua.createBrowserTab("iab", "https://example.com", { visible: true })` call succeeded and initialized the local Codex In-app Browser. Navigation, accessibility observation, and a screenshot of a real page then succeeded. The refreshed inventory exposed IAB while the apps inventory remained empty. Browser access is therefore working through IAB in this tested task.
- Attempting the optional documented `cua.listWindows()` observation returned `TypeError: cua.listWindows is not a function`. With no native app/window inventory and no native initialization tool, native desktop observation/control could not be started.
- A separate Chrome test returned `Browser is not available: chrome`. That is a separate browser availability result, not the native desktop issue reported here.

The computer owner reports that native Computer Use previously worked in ordinary local chats on this machine while delegated tasks did not. That is historical owner-reported evidence; an ordinary local native session was not personally retested on this same build during this check.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Connect and authorize a Windows computer in the desktop app, with Computer Use enabled.
2. From a cloud chat/dot, start a fresh local task on that computer requesting a read-only check of native Windows app/window observation and the supported local browser.
3. Read the installed Computer Use skill and inspect the tools actually exposed to the delegated task. Check whether its documented `node_repl` / `@oai/sky` initialization route is callable.
4. Run `await cua.getState()` through the exposed `cua_repl`. In the tested task, native apps were absent from inventory and native APIs were declared disabled. The optional window-list function was absent.
5. Independently try the supported IAB entry point above, then observe the returned tab and refresh inventory. In this check, IAB initialization and page observation succeeded, while native apps remained unavailable.

These are generic steps describing the observed session, not a claim that every Windows task reproduces the limitation. No clean-install reproduction or fresh same-build ordinary-local/native comparison has been established.

items.title: [Scheduled tasks] Explicit JST request resolved as UTC, causing a 9-hour delay and missed run

labels.name: bug

items.body:
## Summary

A Japanese user working consistently in Japan Standard Time (Asia/Tokyo) explicitly requested a scheduled action at 18:15 and 18:21 JST on 2026-10-06. The agent created a scheduled task using a timezone-less RRULE. The stored next-run timestamp resolved to 18:15 UTC, which is 03:15 JST on the following day. The requested times passed without any execution.

This caused a time-sensitive public-content update to be missed after the assistant had explicitly assured the user that it would run at the requested JST time.

## Environment

- Windows time zone: Asia/Tokyo
- ChatGPT desktop: 1.2026.190.0
- Codex desktop: 26.915.4065.0
- Codex CLI: 0.155.0-alpha.9.2
- Task/session ID: 01a1077f-31c3-7780-9faa-4a829310f909
- Automation ID: r1k5a1l1

## Evidence

- User-requested schedule: 2026-10-06 18:15 and 18:21 JST
- Stored RRULE: `FREQ=DAILY;BYHOUR=18;BYMINUTE=15,21;BYSECOND=0;COUNT=2`
- No timezone or `TZID` was stored with the RRULE.
- Stored `next_run_at`: `1791310559000`
- Converted timestamp:
  - `2026-10-06 18:15:59 UTC`
  - `2026-10-07 03:15:59 JST`
- Offset from the requested local time: exactly +9 hours
- `last_run_at`: null
- Run-history count: 0

The affected automation was paused after the mismatch was discovered to prevent a late duplicate execution.

## Root cause assessment

The immediate agent error was generating a bare RRULE even though the user explicitly specified Japan time, and then reporting success without checking the persisted resolved next-run time.

There is also a product/API reliability problem: the scheduling interface accepted an ambiguous timezone-less RRULE without requiring a timezone, without rejecting the ambiguity, and without making the resolved local execution time prominent enough to force verification before assuring the user.

This report does not claim that every OpenAI scheduled task is always interpreted as UTC. It reports the observed result for this automation: the persisted next-run timestamp was aligned to the RRULE hour in UTC rather than the user-requested JST hour.

## Expected behavior

When a user explicitly states a timezone, scheduled-task creation should preserve it and resolve the next run in that timezone. If the scheduling backend cannot do so, creation should fail clearly instead of silently shifting the time.

## Requested improvements

1. Add a required IANA timezone field to the scheduled-task creation/update API, or require an explicit `TZID` for calendar rules.
2. Reject timezone-less RRULEs when the user prompt or environment contains an explicit timezone.
3. Return the resolved `next_run_at` in both UTC and the user's local timezone from the creation/update call.
4. Require the agent to compare the resolved next run with the requested date, time, and timezone before confirming that scheduling succeeded.
5. Display a clear warning when the resolved execution time differs from the user's stated local time.
6. Add tests covering UTC-positive zones, especially Asia/Tokyo, and non-English conversations.
7. Provide a visible failure or missed-run notification when a promised scheduled action does not start at the requested time.

## User impact and severity

This is a high-severity trust and reliability issue. A nine-hour shift can cause missed publication deadlines, financial or operational actions at the wrong time, and duplicate or late execution. The risk is amplified because the assistant may confidently restate the requested local time even when the persisted schedule disagrees.

Please treat this as a scheduling safety issue and improve both the scheduling API contract and the post-creation verification behavior.

items.body:
## Summary
The ChatGPT desktop app with Codex repeatedly freezes or crashes on an Apple Silicon Mac with 16GB RAM. The ChatGPT process has reportedly grown from 5.76GB to approximately 14GB. Closing the app relieves the system memory pressure. This prevents reliable use of Codex.

## Environment from the analyzed crash report
- App: ChatGPT; bundle ID: com.openai.codex
- App version: 26.930.51102 (build 13100)
- macOS: 26.6.2 (25G83)
- Hardware: Mac17,4; ARM64; 16GB RAM
- Observed October 5–6, 2026, Israel time (UTC+3)

## Observed sequence — not a deterministic reproduction
1. Open the app and run a task using the built-in browser to perform actions in a signed-in web application.
2. In one monitored run, a single browser task was initially stable: Codex (Service) fluctuated around 0.6–1GB, while ChatGPT was around 0.3–0.4GB.
3. After starting another task concurrently, a screenshot showed ChatGPT at **7.93GB** and Codex (Renderer) at **2.55GB**, with yellow memory pressure and 3.03GB swap used.
4. After closing the app, total system memory usage fell from 14.23GB to approximately 6–7GB and memory pressure returned to green.
5. Further app crashes occurred. Earlier failures were also reported during simple messaging, so concurrency is not established as a necessary trigger.

Expected: tasks should run without sustained memory growth that makes the system unresponsive or terminates the app.

## Troubleshooting already performed
- Force quit and reopen; restarted the Mac twice.
- Checked for updates; no update was offered.
- Downloaded and ran the official installer again. It downloaded and automatically opened the app. Exact replacement behavior and the resulting version were not independently verified. The problem subsequently recurred.
- Backed up local Codex data and compared file contents, excluding Finder .DS_Store metadata and the runtime ipc directory. No content differences were reported for the compared files.
- No application-data reset or deletion was performed.

## Crash evidence
Report: ChatGPT-2026-10-06-075450.ips

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Process launch | 2026-10-06 07:41:52 +0300 |
| Crash capture | 2026-10-06 07:54:45 +0300 |
| Exception | EXC_BREAKPOINT (SIGTRAP) |
| Termination | SIGNAL 5 |
| Faulting thread | 0, CrBrowserMain |
| Framework | Codex Framework 154.0.8037.98 |
| Framework UUID | 4c4c4451-5555-3144-a1c5-16973e763bc6 |
| Top frame image offset | 0x8f2fe48 |
| Nearby frames | 0x8f2fe60, 0x8f2fe7c, 0x8f32768, 0x8f302fc |

**Technical interpretation, not an official diagnosis:** A prior analysis of an October 5 crash and a matching framework binary identified the same termination offset as consistent with an allocation-failure path in Chromium/PartitionAlloc. The October 6 report has the same framework UUID and termination offset, but faults on CrBrowserMain rather than Chrome_IOThread. Large symbolication offsets make the displayed function names unreliable for identifying the original operation. This does not identify the source of memory growth or establish a memory leak.

## Corresponding app-log observations
Before the October 6 07:54 crash, the matching app log records built-in browser handoff/route failures, ResizeObserver errors, and internal requests taking approximately 85–101 seconds. These may be symptoms of the slowdown; causality is unknown.

## Incident context and request
The public Work Mode incident lists Codex in ChatGPT Desktop as affected, but does not explicitly identify macOS memory growth or allocation-failure crashes:
https://status.openai.com/incidents/01M45E0JFFJZ6EQ3BWYPW74R2Z

Please clarify whether these symptoms are related to that incident or require separate investigation, and advise on a workaround that preserves local chats and projects.

Crash reports and corresponding app logs are retained locally. This initial public report intentionally omits raw logs, conversation IDs, account details, machine identifiers, and session transcripts. Please advise which further sanitized diagnostics would be useful.

items.body:
### What variant of Codex are you using?

Codex CLI 0.160.0, Default mode.

### What problem are you seeing?

When Codex asks a clarification or implementation-choice question, it may continue planning or coding before I answer. In many cases it proceeds with its own default assumption.

This is especially problematic when the default assumption is not the approach I want. By the time I return and answer the question, Codex may already have inspected more files, written code, or otherwise continued down the wrong path. I then have to stop it, explain the intended choice, undo/rework the implementation, and run the task again.

This is not only a workflow/UX problem: **it causes avoidable token/usage consumption.** Work performed after an unanswered decision point can be entirely wasted, and correcting that work consumes additional usage again.

I remember earlier Codex CLI behavior feeling much safer here: when an important question was asked, I could answer it before dependent implementation continued.

### Current workaround

I added instructions to my `AGENTS.md` telling Codex that when it asks a question affecting implementation, it must stop and wait for my response and must not continue planning, editing files, or running dependent implementation commands.

This reduces the problem, but I don't think prompt instructions should be the primary mechanism for an execution-control guarantee. It also costs context and may not be reliable if the runtime treats the question as non-blocking.

### Expected behavior

If Codex asks a question whose answer materially affects the implementation, dependent work should pause until I explicitly answer or cancel the question.

Ideally there should be a persistent setting such as:

- **Always wait for my answer**
- or a config option making user-input questions blocking / disabling auto-resolution

Optional/non-critical questions can remain asynchronous, but Codex should not choose an implementation branch on the user's behalf after explicitly asking them to choose.

### Why this matters

A wrong automatic choice has a multiplicative cost:

1. Codex spends usage implementing an assumption I did not approve.
2. I have to interrupt or wait for it to finish.
3. Codex then spends more usage reverting/reworking the implementation.
4. The conversation accumulates additional context from work that should never have happened.

For users with usage limits, this makes the current behavior materially expensive, not merely inconvenient.

### Related issues

This appears related to:

- #37472 — Allow `request_user_input` in Default mode to wait indefinitely
- #43759 — Restore blocking control for `request_user_input` independently of Plan mode
- #34455 — Make `request_user_input` timeout duration and timeout behavior configurable
- #44833 — Support blocking structured questions in Codex's default mode

Those issues cover blocking/timeout semantics. I am filing this report to highlight the **CLI 0.160.0 user impact and the avoidable usage/token cost when Codex continues into the wrong implementation before the user answers.**

If this should be consolidated into one of the existing issues, please feel free to close/link it there.

items.body:
Guten Tag,

ich möchte einen schwerwiegenden Fehler bei der Übergabe einer laufenden Aufgabe von einem normalen ChatGPT-Chat an WORK melden.

In einem längeren Gespräch wurde gemeinsam ein komplexes WordPress-Snippet entwickelt. Der vollständige Ausgangscode, bereits getestete Funktionen und weitere vereinbarte Anforderungen waren im ursprünglichen Gespräch vorhanden.

Beim Wechsel zu WORK wurde jedoch nur ein stark verkürzter Ausschnitt der Unterhaltung übertragen beziehungsweise abrufbar gemacht. Der dort arbeitende Assistent erhielt lediglich die letzten wenigen Nachrichten und bemerkte zunächst nicht zuverlässig, dass wesentliche Teile des Kontexts fehlten.

Die Folgen waren erheblich:

Der funktionierende Ausgangscode V2.1 war nicht mehr verfügbar.

Ein bereits vorhandenes TestSnippet wurde zunächst nicht gefunden.

Zuvor vereinbarte Funktionen gingen verloren.

Der Assistent rekonstruierte eine neue Version, obwohl die geforderte exakte Übernahme ohne Originalcode nicht möglich war.

Die erzeugte Datei enthielt zunächst nicht einmal den für dieses Projekt üblichen vollständigen Snippet-Header.

Erst ein von mir selbst erstelltes SQL-Backup rettete den vollständigen Ausgangscode.

Ohne dieses Backup wäre die gemeinsam erarbeitete und funktionierende Grundlage verloren gewesen.

Besonders problematisch ist, dass der Wechsel zu WORK dem Benutzer als Lösung für längere oder komplexere Aufgaben empfohlen wurde, ohne klar darauf hinzuweisen, dass der vollständige Gesprächskontext möglicherweise nicht übernommen wird. Ein Benutzer muss sich darauf verlassen können, dass entweder der gesamte relevante Kontext übertragen wird oder dass der Assistent eindeutig meldet, welche Inhalte fehlen, bevor er Dateien verändert oder neue Versionen erstellt.

Ich erwarte deshalb folgende Verbesserungen:

Vollständige und überprüfbare Kontextübergabe zwischen ChatGPT und WORK.

Eine deutliche Warnung, wenn nur ein begrenzter Gesprächsausschnitt verfügbar ist.

Keine Behauptung, eine Aufgabe basiere auf einem früheren Code, wenn dieser Code tatsächlich nicht vorliegt.

Automatische Prüfung, ob referenzierte Dateien und frühere Codefassungen wirklich verfügbar sind.

Klare Anzeige, welche Nachrichten, Anhänge und Dateien bei einer Übergabe fehlen.

Keine Empfehlung zum Wechsel des Arbeitsbereichs, wenn dadurch ein Kontextverlust droht.

Eine zuverlässige Möglichkeit, umfangreiche fertige Dateien zu erzeugen, ohne dass Inhalte abgeschnitten werden.

Dieser Vorfall hat unnötig viel Zeit gekostet und hätte ohne mein eigenes Backup zum vollständigen Verlust der Arbeitsgrundlage geführt. Bitte leiten Sie diese Meldung an die zuständigen Entwickler für ChatGPT WORK, Kontextübertragung und Gesprächsreferenzen weiter.

Mit freundlichen Grüßen

Peter Roskothen

items.body:
## Summary

In a Linux Codex-managed shell, even a read-only user-systemd query fails with:

```text
Failed to connect to user scope bus via local transport: No data available
```

The user session bus and user service manager are responding. The failing private-manager connection succeeds at the socket level, but `SO_PEERCRED` reports peer PID `0`. This appears to be a PID-namespace interoperability limitation, rather than a stopped user bus.

Please treat this as a compatibility report, not a proven regression. I am not requesting removal of sandbox isolation or suppression of systemd's credential checks.

## Environment observed

- Installed CLI: `codex-cli 0.160.1`.
- OS visible to the shell: Ubuntu 26.04.1 LTS, x86_64.
- Kernel: `7.0.0-34-generic`.
- User service manager: `259.5-0ubuntu3.4`.
- Execution policy: workspace-write, no approval escalation, network enabled.
- `/proc/1/status` identifies `codex` as PID 1 in the execution namespace.
- The installed CLI version is not proof of the version of the managed executor serving this session; that executor version has not been established.
- Subscription, model identity and terminal emulator are not established by these diagnostics.

## Read-only reproduction in the affected shell

```sh
systemctl --user show --property=Version

busctl --user get-property   org.freedesktop.systemd1   /org/freedesktop/systemd1   org.freedesktop.systemd1.Manager Version

strace -e trace=connect,getsockopt   systemctl --user show --property=Version
```

Observed: the `systemctl` query exits 1 with the error above, while the `busctl` query exits 0 and returns:

```text
s "259.5-0ubuntu3.4"
```

Relevant trace excerpt, with the local numeric user/group identifiers replaced by placeholders:

```text
connect(3, {sa_family=AF_UNIX, sun_path="/run/user/<UID>/systemd/private"}, 39) = 0
getsockopt(3, SOL_SOCKET, SO_PEERCRED, {pid=0, uid=<UID>, gid=<GID>}, [12]) = 0
...
getsockopt(3, SOL_SOCKET, SO_PEERCRED, {pid=0, uid=<UID>, gid=<GID>}, [12]) = 0
Failed to connect to user scope bus via local transport: No data available
+++ exited with 1 +++
```

The original trace used an ordinary numeric runtime-directory path; its length field is preserved from that trace. A separate read-only public-bus query also confirmed that the existing resource-control slice is active.

## Impact

A local managed launcher using `systemd-run --user --scope --slice=<resource-slice>` fails before launching its workload. The same connection error therefore blocks resource-governed worker execution. The simplified read-only reproduction above does not require that launcher or creating any unit.

## Source evidence and limits

- [Codex 0.160.1 bubblewrap argument construction](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.160.1/codex-rs/linux-sandbox/src/bwrap.rs): constructs `--unshare-pid` unless the internal inherit-PID-namespace option is selected.
- [systemd peer-credential helper](https://github.com/systemd/systemd/blob/v259/src/basic/socket-util.c#L780-L800): rejects an invalid peer PID with `ENODATA`, explicitly noting namespace-related suppression.
- [systemd user-manager connection](https://github.com/systemd/systemd/blob/v259/src/shared/bus-util.c#L247-L279): connects through the private socket and runs that check.

These observations establish the immediate failure mechanism. They do not establish which executor/outer sandbox layer introduced PID isolation, or prove that this previously worked. A normal-terminal A/B comparison and a standalone `codex sandbox linux` reproduction have not been performed.

## Requested outcome

Please clarify the supported integration for user-systemd/resource-governed jobs from the Linux sandbox. If this interaction is unsupported, expose an actionable namespace-specific diagnostic or documentation rather than letting an otherwise healthy user bus appear broken. Any supported integration should preserve filesystem, PID and resource-control security boundaries.

No service restart, credential-check suppression, sandbox bypass or alternate unmanaged workload launch was used.

## Related report / duplicate search

[Issue #23687](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/23687) discusses misleading host diagnostics from sandbox-distorted observations; this report adds a specific systemd connection failure and syscall evidence. Searches for `ENODATA`, `peercred`, and combinations of systemd/systemctl with namespace terms did not reveal an exact matching report; that search is not an exhaustive absence claim.

### Summary

I am trying to verify the supported serialization contract for Codex Cloud task diffs.

On two bounded Cloud tasks, the task reached `READY`, but `codex cloud diff <TASK_ID> --attempt 1` returned no diff. The two tasks used different file-mutation producers:

1. a tracked-file mutation through ordinary shell I/O;
2. a tracked-file mutation explicitly requested through Codex `apply_patch`.

The goal here is **not** to report that the workspace definitely mutated. The observable fact is narrower: after `READY`, the task-details surface exposed no serialized diff that the CLI could retrieve.

### Public-source trace

At public source revision:

`822e58cc3d666166c7446c5b1ea2e52f5d09594c`

the following client/core contracts are visible:

- `codex-rs/core/src/tools/handlers/apply_patch.rs` produces an `AppliedPatchDelta`.
- `codex-rs/core/src/tools/events.rs` feeds that delta into `TurnDiffTracker` and emits `EventMsg::TurnDiff`.
- `codex-rs/core/src/turn_diff_tracker.rs` builds the unified diff for committed `apply_patch` changes.
- `codex-rs/backend-client/src/types.rs` decodes `current_diff_task_turn` / `current_assistant_turn`, and accepts non-empty diff items of type `output_diff` or `pr.output_diff`.
- `codex-rs/cloud-tasks-client/src/http.rs` reads task details and returns only the backend-provided unified diff.
- `codex-rs/cloud-tasks/src/lib.rs` powers the native `cloud diff` command from that backend diff.

What I could not locate in public source is the server-side bridge:

`Cloud worker TurnDiff -> server transport/persistence -> current_diff_task_turn/output_diff`

### Questions for the server/task owner

Could you clarify the supported contract for that bridge?

1. Is a `TurnDiff` emitted by the Cloud worker expected to be persisted into task-details as `current_diff_task_turn.output_items[type=output_diff]` (or equivalent `pr.output_diff`)?
2. If yes, what conditions can cause that diff to be dropped, filtered, or omitted?
3. Is `READY + no serialized diff` a valid terminal state even when the worker workspace may have changed?
4. Is there a supported read-only CLI/API surface for historical task worklog/tool events that is independent of assistant-text rendering and `output_diff`?
5. If the bridge is implemented outside the public repo, is there a public contract or source pointer we should rely on when building verification tooling?

### Why this matters

The current CLI error says:

`No diff available for task ...; it may still be running.`

When status is independently confirmed as `READY`, that message is ambiguous. A documented distinction between:

- no workspace mutation,
- mutation occurred but no `TurnDiff`,
- `TurnDiff` emitted but not persisted,
- persisted diff not exposed by the CLI

would make Cloud-task verification substantially more reliable.

There were **9 primary-state file replacements**, and the main process disk-write counter increased by **69,009,408 bytes**. **3 replacements had identical parsed JSON before and after.** The other replacements coincided with these fields:

- `electron-persisted-atom-state/primary-aeon-selection-v1/response/profile/avatar_url`
- `electron-persisted-atom-state/cloud-aeon-sidebar-cache-v1/profilesByThreadId/<redacted>/avatar_url`
- The same sidebar profiles' `messaging_room_preview`
- `electron-persisted-atom-state/cloud-aeon-sidebar-cache-v1/refreshStartedAtMs`

The affected files are:

```text
~/.codex/.codex-global-state.json
~/.codex/.codex-global-state.json.bak
```

Each is approximately **3.83 MB**. One full primary-plus-backup save accounted for **7,667,712 bytes** in this environment; the nine-save window's total exactly matched nine times that amount. Poll-level counter deltas can split the two file writes, so individual poll deltas are not presented as complete per-save attribution.

| Approx. elapsed seconds | Observed primary-state saves |
| --- | --- |
| 3.73 / 4.40 / 5.37 | Unchanged JSON / primary-profile avatar / sidebar cache |
| 84.03 / 84.71 / 85.99 | Unchanged JSON / primary-profile avatar / sidebar cache |
| 154.31 / 155.14 / 156.10 | Unchanged JSON / primary-profile avatar / sidebar cache |

The large, unchanged payload includes:

| Top-level state field | Serialized bytes |
| --- | ---: |
| `mcp-server-tools-cache-v2` | 1,448,123 |
| `mcp-extension-sidebar-catalog` | 1,357,425 |
| `mcp-global-entrypoints-v2` | 279,621 |

These total approximately **3.09 MB / 80.6%** of the state. Their contents were not observed changing in the idle sample; they amplify the writes caused by other small updates.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

Observed reproduction with the existing account/state, rather than a clean-profile minimal reproducer:

1. Run the macOS desktop app with Your dot/cloud-agent sidebar data available. In this environment, installed MCP/plugin catalogs make the global-state JSON approximately 3.8 MB.
2. Identify the main `ChatGPT` executable process, rather than a renderer, the CLI or the Rust app-server.
3. Record its disk bytes written in Activity Monitor, or use `proc_pid_rusage` with `RUSAGE_INFO_V2` and `ri_diskio_byteswritten`.
4. For about three minutes, observe the primary global-state file's inode/mtime. On replacement, compare the previous and current parsed JSON **locally**, recording only changed field names and sizes. Do not publish the raw state.
5. Avoid typing, opening panels or switching chats during the idle observation. Observe background profile/sidebar cache changes and occasional semantically unchanged replacements.
6. Correlate those replacements with the main process's disk-write counter and the full-sized primary/backup files.

The diagnostic collection did not manually modify state files or the app bundle during either measurement window; the app continued its normal persistence. Session IDs and raw cache values are omitted because this is a desktop persistence report and those values can contain private data.

### What is the expected behavior?

- Skip persistence when serialized/semantic state has not changed.
- Avoid rewriting several megabytes of unrelated catalogs plus a full backup for every small, transient profile/sidebar-cache update.
- Consider persisting large catalogs separately and batching/throttling derived cache updates while preserving necessary state durability.

### Additional information

**Follow-up on the official reinstalled build 13232:** a **180.01-second** observation still recorded **23,003,136 bytes** and **3 primary-state saves**: one tab-route change, one primary-profile avatar update and one cloud-sidebar cache update. This window included a UI-state change, so it is **not a controlled idle-only sample** and should not be used to infer an improvement from the older version's total. It confirms that small cache updates still coincide with full-state persistence in the newer official installation.

Read-only inspection of the installed build 13100's bundled JavaScript found the following path:

- `persisted-atom-update` -> `updatePersistedAtomState` in `.vite/build/main-C7cfj__D.js` -> the global state store's `set`.
- In `.vite/build/startup-requirements-CLgOyk51.js`, the state store serializes the complete map and atomically replaces the primary file and then its `.bak` with the same complete JSON, with a 500 ms debounce for atom updates and no serialized-content equality guard at that saving layer.
- The primary-profile and cloud-sidebar query paths in `webview/assets/app-shared-9d148924be0b.js` update the persisted keys listed above after refreshes.

**Limits of the diagnosis:** the upstream event starting each refresh and the call stacks submitting identical values were not captured. The observed 70–80-second gaps do not establish a fixed polling timer. The byte counts are macOS process disk-I/O counters, not SSD-controller physical-write measurements. This is an existing-profile observation; background account activity has not been independently isolated.

Related reports checked before filing:

- #35401 concerns the Rust CLI/app-server's separate `cache/remote_plugin_catalog` files, rather than the desktop Electron global-state files measured here.

Could maintainers investigate deduplication and persistence granularity for these desktop cache updates? ```

### What issue are you seeing?

The whole desktop app repeatedly became unresponsive about 30 seconds after launch/use, interrupting clicks, typing and active work. This persisted across repeated relaunches, plugin isolation, a machine reboot and stopping Time Machine.

The user reports this did not happen before an attempted external-drive migration on October 5, 2026. That attempt failed **before copying or cutover** because a Chrome native messaging helper reappeared with source paths open. The original home and database location remained active; seven saved startup files matched their originals. The temporal association is recorded, but no causal mechanism connecting the attempted migration to the freeze has been established.

**New mitigation evidence:** while the app was fully stopped, removing only the derived cloud-sidebar cache key from the global UI-state file was followed by user-observed responsiveness beyond the previous failure interval. A few initial slow keystrokes remained. This is a promising workaround, not a demonstrated permanent fix or proof that the cache was corrupt.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

Observed incident sequence, rather than a fresh minimal reproduction:

1. Launch the desktop app with the existing persisted state and conversation/sidebar history.
2. Initially interact normally.
3. Within approximately 30 seconds, the user reports the whole app freezes.
4. Relaunch; the freeze recurs. The user clarified this also occurs when compaction is not running.
5. Disable failing custom integrations and relaunch: the whole-app freeze still occurs.
6. Reboot the machine and stop Time Machine: the whole-app freeze still occurs.
7. Fully quit the app and preserve a recovery copy of the specific cached value.
8. Remove only:
   `electron-persisted-atom-state["cloud-aeon-sidebar-cache-v1"]`
   from `$CODEX_HOME/.codex-global-state.json`, leaving other state unchanged.
9. Reopen: the user reports no freeze beyond the interval at which it had previously occurred.

The cache-reset script checked that app processes were stopped, checked the volume identity, wrote atomically, and verified all other JSON state remained semantically unchanged. No conversations, SQLite data, credentials or other preferences were cleared. This manual diagnostic edit is **not an app-supported safe mode**. The saved cache has not been restored to reproduce the failure, and an additional ordinary quit/reopen stability test remains pending.

A long-running chat was near its automatic-compaction threshold (latest retained pre-reset sample: 242,200 usage tokens versus a 244,800 threshold; effective context window 258,400). The freeze was not limited to that chat or to compaction. A later persisted compaction record and completed turn confirm that compaction eventually succeeded. Private conversation/session IDs are omitted.

### What is the expected behavior?

Persisted sidebar/history state should load without blocking app input. A cached-state loading failure should be recoverable without manually editing global state or clearing conversation data. An app-supported way to reset only derived UI caches would help diagnosis.

### Additional information

#### Diagnostics and isolation

- The removed cache was approximately 2.83 MB within a roughly 3.5 MB global UI-state file. Its size alone does not establish corruption.
- A launch logged 464 `thread/read` responses across 434 distinct chats. This is aggregate activity, not proof that sidebar work caused the freeze.
- Repeated `ResizeObserver loop completed with undelivered notifications.` errors were present; an earlier run logged 66 in five seconds. These are generic layout errors, not evidence of native notification delivery or a proven causal chain.
- Several custom MCP/plugin initialization failures were separately reproduced. Repairing a relative computer-use executable/cwd and disabling the failing integrations cleared connector discovery failures during later captured launches, but did not resolve the user-observed freeze. A newer enabled plugin entry was subsequently disabled as well, without resolution.
- Activity Monitor during the incident showed approximately 90.84% system CPU idle; app main 7.9%, primary renderer 10.6%, backend 1.6%. Another earlier main-process CPU spike was transient. Memory-pressure inspection reported 93% free. No sustained CPU or memory exhaustion was demonstrated.
- Short main/renderer/backend samples mainly contained ordinary wait states. They did not identify a specific deadlock or blocking function and cannot independently prove responsiveness.
- Earlier state-database integrity and foreign-key checks passed. Historical missing rollout references were separately investigated; no new database corruption or causal connection to this freeze was demonstrated.
- Direct app UI automation was unavailable, so freeze/improvement assessments are the user's observations. One process-presence result conflicted with the user's confirmed open window and was discarded.
- The cache-reset outcome followed other interventions and reduced background activity; this was not a controlled reversal experiment.

- [#50984](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/50984): same app build and approximately 30-second restored-window freeze. That report has sustained renderer CPU saturation and a fresh-window workaround; those findings have not been established here. This report adds the single-key sidebar-cache intervention.
- [#40559](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/40559): persisted file-tab state causes repeated renderer freezes, recoverable by removing a specific global-state key. Different key/trigger/build; shared cause unconfirmed.

- [#51073](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/51073): same-build stored-notification/Markdown parser CPU hang. No problematic Markdown input or equivalent regex stack has been isolated in this incident.

Searches for the exact `cloud-aeon-sidebar-cache-v1` key returned no existing issue. These are potentially related symptoms, not confirmed duplicates.

Could maintainers investigate restoration/reconciliation of this cached sidebar state and advise on a supported trace or cache-only recovery procedure? A fuller local RCA and diagnostic samples are retained. Raw logs, cached cloud data, conversation contents, credentials, account identifiers and personal filesystem paths are not attached.

items.body:
## Summary

On **ChatGPT Web**, a project folder that has been pinned can disappear from the **Projects** tab/interface instead of remaining visible in the complete projects list.

The project itself still exists and remains accessible through **Pinned**. The problem is the Projects interface no longer shows that same project once it is pinned.

Pinning should be a presentation/priority state, not a filter that removes the project from the canonical project browser.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Open ChatGPT Web.
2. Create or use an existing ChatGPT Project.
3. Pin that project.
4. Confirm it appears in the **Pinned** section.
5. Open the **Projects** tab/interface.
6. Observe that the pinned project is missing from the Projects list.

## Expected behavior

The **Projects** interface should show all accessible projects, regardless of pin state.

A pinned project should therefore:

- remain visible in **Projects**;
- also appear in **Pinned** as a shortcut/high-priority item;
- keep the same project identity and contents in both representations;
- not require unpinning just to make it visible in the Projects browser again.

Pinning should affect prominence/order, not membership in the project catalog.

## Actual behavior

After a project is pinned, it is omitted from the **Projects** tab/interface.

This makes **Pinned** and **Projects** behave like mutually exclusive buckets even though pinning is only an organizational state.

## Why this matters

The Projects tab should be the canonical place to browse the user's projects. If pinned projects are filtered out:

- the Projects view is incomplete;
- users can reasonably think projects are missing or deleted;
- project discoverability depends on remembering pin state;
- a navigation preference unexpectedly changes catalog visibility.

A user should be able to open **Projects** and reliably find every project whether pinned or unpinned.

## Engineering angle / area to inspect

Without asserting the root cause, this looks like a **client-side filtering / collection-membership bug**.

Useful checks may include:

- whether the Projects query or selector excludes records with a pinned/sidebar-section flag;
- whether pinning mutates a section enum that is incorrectly treated as exclusive membership;
- whether the Projects UI is consuming an `unpinnedProjects` collection rather than the canonical all-projects collection;
- whether the same project ID remains in the account/project state while only the rendered collection changes;
- whether pin/unpin invalidation updates one sidebar section but incorrectly removes the item from another.

A regression test could create several projects, pin a subset, and assert that **all project IDs remain visible in Projects while the pinned subset also appears in Pinned**.

## Environment

- Surface: **ChatGPT Web**
- Browser: **Google Chrome 154**
- OS: **Windows 10 x64**
- Affected UI: **Projects / Pinned sidebar navigation**
- Observed: **2026-10-06**

## Duplicate review

I searched the public `openai/codex` tracker for pinned-project and Projects-visibility issues.

Related but not identical reports include:

- #38943: ChatGPT Web pin/sidebar organization state can hide unrelated Recents.
- #38486: a pinned project folder cannot be moved back to Projects on macOS.
- #50161: a ChatGPT project visible/pinned on web is missing from the Codex desktop project registry.
- #50773: request to browse all Codex projects regardless of pinning in the Codex sidebar.

This report is specifically about **ChatGPT Web's Projects interface omitting a project because that project is pinned**.

items.title: [Linux Desktop] Clicking web Work completion notification opens web chat inside Codex project view

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

labels.name: session
labels.description: Issues involving session (thread) management, resuming, forking, naming, archiving

items.body:
## Summary

Clicking a desktop completion notification for a separate ChatGPT Work browser conversation opens that web conversation inside the desktop Codex project view. Both user messages and assistant replies appear verbatim in desktop formatting. The desktop composer can then send messages to the same web conversation.

The user has now identified the notification click as the trigger: receiving the notification alone does not replace the displayed local project chat. According to the latest test, the unexpected conversation view does not occur without clicking the notification. This supersedes the earlier hypothesis of spontaneous cross-conversation display replacement.

Reselecting the intended local project chat restores its original execution report, even if that local chat previously appeared to be the current chat.

## Environment

- Linux desktop; exact application version has not been collected.
- Desktop app in its Codex area, with local project conversations.
- Separate ChatGPT Work conversation in a browser, created independently at a different time.
- Observed repeatedly on October 6, 2026.

## User-reported reproduction

1. Select a local project chat in the desktop Codex area.
2. Keep the separate Work conversation open in the browser.
3. Send a message in the web conversation and receive the assistant reply.
4. The desktop application generates a completion notification associated with that web reply.
5. Leave the notification unclicked: the selected local project chat retains its contents. The user tested this with a different local project selected.
6. Click the completion notification.
7. The desktop Codex pane now displays the web conversation, including both sides of the conversation and its attachments, using the desktop application's formatting.
8. During this view, no local project chat appears selected in the sidebar. The surrounding navigation still exposes the Codex area and local projects. The controls differ from the original project view: web content or no title, Custom in the selector, and web attachments in Sources.
9. Writing/sending a message in this desktop view reaches the web Work conversation, according to the user.
10. Reselect the intended local project chat: its original execution report and project view return.

The user regards the notification click as the reliably identified trigger. The assistant has inspected screenshots but has not independently operated the desktop, traced events, or instrumented the routing.

## Input routing and scope

The user explicitly clarifies that the observed conversation-content flow is one-way: web Work conversation → desktop Codex view. They have not observed the original local Codex agent's replies or history appearing in the web conversation.

The desktop-composer observation below concerns typing into the notification-opened web conversation view. It must not be described as the original local coding agent's content leaking back into the browser.

The reported input direction after notification activation is desktop interface → web Work conversation. The user does not report the reverse: browser messages being submitted to the original local coding conversation.

This is compatible with the notification opening the web conversation as the active desktop conversation, rather than copying text into the local coding agent's context. It is an interpretation, not a verified implementation-level explanation.

There is no observed evidence here of leaked local-agent context, permanently merged histories, or unintended local project actions. The internal cause and whether cross-surface notification navigation itself is intended remain unverified.

## Notification evidence

A screenshot captures a native toast branded "ChatGPT", labelled "Turn complete", containing the exact assistant response shown in the web conversation. The user identifies the desktop application as its source and reports no configured notification hook. The source process has not been independently traced.

A separate Chrome site-permissions screenshot shows chatgpt.com notifications set to "Ask (default)", not "Allow". The user reports never receiving or approving a browser notification-permission request. Browser notification permission must therefore be described as ungranted/default Ask, not explicitly blocked.

## Expected behavior

If notification activation intentionally opens a web Work conversation in the shared desktop client, the interface should clearly identify that conversation and its mode. Conversation identity, navigation/sidebar state, and composer destination should be consistent and unambiguous.

Reselecting the local project chat restores the intended local view, but the notification-opened view initially led the user to believe that web content was appearing in the local coding conversation. The report requests review of that navigation and identification behavior; it does not establish that all cross-surface notifications are inherently erroneous.

## Impact

The user reports closing the desktop application because of the recurring notifications associated with web replies.

The user had difficulty identifying which conversation and execution environment were active after notification activation. The local coding project has broad execution permissions, which made this ambiguity concerning.

## Related reports

- https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/39622 — ChatGPT/Codex windows showing the wrong conversation on Windows.
- https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/39191 — Windows desktop displaying content from another thread among other thread-state failures.

Both involve similar visible symptoms on Windows. This report now identifies a notification-click trigger in the Linux/browser workflow. A shared root cause is unconfirmed.

## Evidence and privacy

User-supplied screenshots were inspected and show the original local project view, the web conversation displayed in desktop formatting, a completion toast matching the web reply, and the Chrome notification setting. Screenshots are not attached publicly because they contain private conversations and project details.

No credentials, account identifiers, thread IDs, private project names, project paths or raw logs are included.

Codex Desktop repeatedly closes during image-based work and can subsequently fail to stay open. Moving the existing `.codex` directory aside and allowing the app to create a fresh one restored usability.

Its `src` is a `data:image/png;base64,...` string of **139,179,370 characters**. The matching original PNG on disk is **104,384,510 bytes**, with dimensions **7168 × 9600**. 2. Attach large PNG images and submit a follow-up. In the preserved failing state, the follow-up is persisted in `queued-follow-ups` with inline base64 image data.
3. The app unexpectedly closes. Relaunching with the same profile may exit again within a few seconds.
4. Preserve/move the existing `.codex` directory and start with a fresh directory. In this case, the app became usable again.

Session IDs, local file paths, prompts and original images are omitted from this public report.

Large image attachments should either be processed successfully or rejected with an actionable error. An attachment or queued message should not leave the app unable to start with the existing profile. Recovery should preserve existing conversations and settings.

**Timeline (UTC, October 5, 2026):**

- Queued follow-up `createdAt`: **06:33:32.509Z**.

labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: app
